text: Scans indicate this habitat is in unusually well-preserved condition despite its abandoned state. There is little evidence of disrepair, parts cannibalization, or even electromagnetic scoring from the nearby stellar body; it appears that even the original paintjob has survived its years in isolation.

There is an unusual delay before salvage operations can commence. Helmet vis-IDs streaming to the bridge indicate an uptick in nervousness amongst your salvors; old spacer wisdom and salvor's tales speak quite ill of the consequences for disturbing uniquely pristine Domain-era finds. Superstition aside, dangerous operations are only made more fraught by unknown variables, and you find your own heart beating just a tick faster than before.

A bark over comms from your operations chief (and a subtle hint at increased hazard pay) and the salvors are on the move. There is no need for demolitions - the station's fully functional airlocks open smoothly to allow entry, and salvors find easily-accessible cargo holds packed with supplies and valuable materials still sealed in their mag-locked cargo containers. You watch incredulously as the first of the containers is scanned for its inventory manifest - but are cut short as alarms suddenly blare both within the station and aboard the bridge.

Ops sounds an immediate emergency evacuation to the salvage team, while your sensors chief begins shouting about energy signatures matching shield and weapon systems activating all over the station. From behind the station's (now understood to be shielded) aft shuttle docks, a fleet of Domain Explorarium drones emerges, burning hard to intercept the fleet.

The pristine station spins idly in front of you. Just behind it, its fleet of guard ships sits, so steady in their watch you'd think them disabled if it weren't for their targeting systems actively scanning you.
The defenders are destroyed. Behind the wreckage, the heavily damaged - but not completely annihilated - station sits idly.

Following some freshly unsubtle promises of hazard pay (and promises of contract terminations should they refuse), your salvage team once again enters the now-battered station. Once again the salvors' tallies begin to roll in, but with an exceptional new find: in the core of the station, well-protected from any battles that may have raged before this, are four pristine combat-capable ships ready for command.
Your fleet approaches the station. Repairs have been put underway, but following the destruction of its defenders it is unlikely it will ever be as flawless as you once found it.
You dock with the station.
You order teams to inspect the cargo storage areas.

script: AddBarEvent EBEbar_start "Sit down with the knight" "At a corner table, you see a lone Knight of Ludd, fingers together like the steeple of a church in half prayer while a simple bowl of simpler tea steams silently in front of them. Watching you, intently, since you walked in." luddicChurchColor

text:
You walk over to parlay with the knight. Their hands, and eyes, remain locked forward as you approach their table. When you draw close enough, an invisible barrier is passed. Their eyes shift to you; their fingers uncurl from their devotion and they sit up straighter than before, raising both arms, sliding their hands into their opposite sleeves.

As you sit down, the knight finally, directly, acknowledges you. "Captain," they state. "Thank you for coming over." Their gaze slides off you for a moment, some errant thought, before they look back with an apologetic frown. "Forgive me, $playerSirOrMadam, if I appeared suspicious. I did not wish to impose."
options: EBEbarKnight_1b:"You got my attention. We'll see if you can keep it."

text: "We will." They reach down to their bowl of steeped tea, crushed leaves of dark emerald gleam floating just under the surface. They take a long, practiced sip, then lay down the bowl and gaze through as they explain their sacred task.

"Already you've drawn our sword, though not much else. I believe Ludd has delivered a blessed opportunity for you to flourish."

They consider their next words.

"The Hegemony. The League. The corporation. Any one of them you could have chosen to fight for." Their shoulders rise with a single, brief chuckle. "Any of them would pay better, yet you choose to crusade with us. Perhaps that's enough."
options:
GreetNeutralCommOptionOne:"The credits are enough."
GreetNeutralCommOptionTwo:"I respond well to incentive."

text: Their cheeks rise into into a knowing smile. "But barely, I'm sure. Thus, this meeting."
"We've noticed."

text:
"You've already proven yourself a capable crusader. More than capable. We considered other names, but, yours was at the top of the list."

The knight pauses for a moment, then offers an assuring smile.

"It was a very short list, captain."

They return to their stone expression. "Obedience, loyalty. Discretion. The Church knows you value all of these things, so we trust you with this."
"You are a friend of the Church, if not in our formal ranks. As a fellow pilgrim, the Church believes you can provide an, independent approach to our situation."
options:
GreetWelcomingOptionOne:"You need someone disposable."
GreetWelcomingOptionTwo:"Not that suspicious when I take off to the end of the sector, is it?"

text:
"No," they answer flatly, "and don't discount yourself. We considered others, fellow brothers 
and sisters. You were still the best suited."
"That reason was brought up. Now then."
"But your faith is-" $heorShe starts, then trails off into something short of a scowl. "Questionable. Your loyalties suspect. At best."
options:
GreetSuspiciousOptionOne:"I'm what you call a \"prodigal child.\""
GreetSuspiciousOptionTwo:"Offering me redemption?"
GreetSuspiciousOptionThree:"My loyalties are perfectly known. They're just not to you."

text:
"I'm not here to judge you, captain; that is for God alone to render, but your transgressions against the Church? Those are simply fact. What I'm offering is, some measure of recompense."

They look off for a moment, and deflate with a sigh. 

"And, of course, compensation."

"Despite the, zeal, of some of our preachers, the road to damnation is much longer than most think. Ludd gives us many, many chances to realize we are astray. And easier to turn back just a few steps down the wrong road. Now, if you would indulge me."

Their lips curl into an empty smirk.

"Honesty. It is a virtue. Keep nurturing it."
"I wish to be honest. Your interpretation of the Word may be more...energetic than the Church approves, but perhaps that's what's needed."

The knight looks out the window, into the old ocean of the void, silent as the steam column from their tea slowly thins.

"There was a mission," they begin. "A task. Mostly holy, to cast down an unholy vessel."

$HeOrShe turns back to you and raises one hand from their sleeve, fingers rolling in vague gesture.

"An Abomination. Forged by Moloch themselves. It matched no records. No blueprints. Nothing in any archive of the Curates Technologia. An unknown demon. Our brothers and sisters were dispatched to destroy it, to smite it in Ludd's name, but." 

The knight's eyes wander to the table. "They never returned. We suspect the worst."

They glance back up and continue. "We need you to confirm the fate of the fleet. And, if possible, find out where the Abomination fled. If the worst has happened, surely our knights at least wounded the thing before falling. You do not have to destroy the machine, if you encounter it. That task will fall to us, once we've gleamed what system it's crawled into. You will, of course, be rewarded generously."
Explain that you're not interested at this time.

Your fleet approaches the Invictus.

It is a hulk ripped apart, spaced cargo and blasted hull floating from its deep innards like metal blubber. For kilometers around, your sensors ping nebulae of gnarled metal and chaff and broken shapes. The remains of other dead Luddic ships, a school of shredded guppies drifting around a dead leviathan.

Your tac officer breaks the silence.

"Captain. All the other ships are just above background temp, but we're still getting thermal from the Invictus. A LOT of thermal. It's, uh, actually getting hotter."

"Aye, captain. Direct hit, looks like. Much longer and she's gonna start glowing, if the heat don't cook off the magazines first. And you'll want to see this."

You're motioned over to their console, where a scanned diagram of the wounded behemoth glows before you. Glowing smears of thermal activity coat its destroyed hull, and your tac officer points to a section that's bluer than the rest.

"One of the crew quarters. Heat hasn't gotten there yet, so we can still see localized low thermals. Barely. We're picking up a few dozen or so, maybe a hundred."

They look up to you, brows raised. "People, $playerSirOrMadam."

The crew hums stirs from their idleness, a dozen orders cruising their way down from the high throne of your bridge. Within minutes a large team of salvors and medics and technicians already assembled, along with a healthy contingent of hardened drones.

The airlock has already been cleared. They await your command.

The team touches off, jumping out from the airlock in pairs until only the drones remain. When they clear the airlock, the drones follow in short order. You select the feed of one of them, choosing it as your avatar as the vaguely square ruin of the Invictus slowly approaches.

A voice crackles into your speakers. The leader of the boarding party.

"Looks like fires on multiple decks."

You can see the scorch marks for yourself on the camera, along with the haze of dappled static; bullets of radiation crawling through the drone's electronic eye.

"Radiation's getting worse." Their tone isn't worried. Not yet. But it is a warning. "If there's people in there, I can't make many guarantees."

Your tac officer's eyes remain on their screen. "Meltdown's accelerating. We can probably slow it down, but not for long. Should I divert the techs, $playerSirOrMadam?"

With a terse order, the command is relayed. A few of the white, bulkier EVA suits and drones peel off from the floating group, headed towards the beast's melting heart. The rest continue, your feed showing the group slowly drifting towards a hallway exposed to the vacuum. At the end, a sealed doorway, snapped tight even against the vacuum. The boarding party swarms near it like curious ants, carefully constructing a makeshift airlock around the door to make entry. 

"Captain," the lead calls.

You simply nod at your second officer, who relays your affirmation. The temporary airlock is engaged, fastened to hull, and the boarding party's lead floats inside, along with your chosen drone.

A sour hiss fills the speakers. You hear voices as white, pressurized gas briefly fogs the lens the drone, then fades to greater shouts.

People.

Faithful of the Luddic church, clad in fatigues of green and emerald and primal suggestions of leaves and trees. They float about the cabin aimlessly, holding to any jutting surface they can, over two hundred eyes locked either on the drone or the boarding lead. Many are wounded. Some mortally. Chapped lips and sweat, so many pale as moon dust. They've been here for days.

One of them, clearly the Knight-Captain of the vessel, floats towards the boarding party leader, eyes bulging with pallid flesh. They back away, pointing instead to the drone. You flick a button, turning on the console's camera to show your face to the weary crew.

"Did the Church send you?" they croak.
"Praise the Creator."

Another Knight half-floats, half-limps over. Their legs is covered in bandaged. Underneath, the seared gore of radiation burns. 

"We did not...fail," they stammer. The mere effort of talking is too much, and they double over in pain. Two ensigns float over to try and pull them away, only for the knight to swat at them like an angry animal.

They turn back to you, brimstone in their eyes. "We did not. Fail," they repeat. The point 
towards the camera, their arm too blistered by the touch of radiation. "We found the demon. 
We engaged it. We hurt it."
options:
EBEInvictusBoardingFiveBonus:"Looks like it won, though."
EBEInvictusBoardingSix:"What happened?"

text:
The knight's eyes grow wide with fury. They push away the nearby ensigns, then impotently throw themselves at your drone in a futile, floating lunge. 

"WE DID NOT FAIL!" they scream. "WE DIDN'T-"

In slow motion, they're tackled by another group of faithful. They wrestle them to the bulkhead, dragging them back to a makeshift infirmity in the corner of the room.

The other knight glances back to your drone. "Forgive them. They have gone through 
much. We all have."
"We were given a mission, captain. A most holy one."

"Then they told you. We set out with a full fleet to smite it. We were...confident, that would be 
enough. It wasn't. The beast danced around us. Like fighting a dozen ships at once. It picked us off, one-by-one. But a few of our salvos went through. We did wound it, captain, but it fled before we could finish it."

They stop speaking, arms falling limp to their sides.

"...Were there any others? On the other ships?"
"Then we have squandered much more than ships. We will face whatever penitence the Church deems fit."

text:
You explain, in vague terms, the ultimate fate of the Luddic Fleet and its survivors.

The knight falls into a grim countenance. "I... I see." A heavy silence takes the air as a prayer is uttered with a bowed head. "May none more trespass, then." They glance up, eyes burning with new fire. "If that is the case..."
"You return. I believe we have something to discuss."

"The Church would not normally trust such a task to a, hm. Layman, but action must be taken. Now, before the monstrosity eludes us."

They gaze up towards the ceiling.

"The abomination must be destroyed. That is your task."
"The Church would not so easily give a task to those outside the knightly orders, but action must be taken swiftly. Will you finish this and hunt down the foul machine?"

"I can't force you. I also can't approve of this...meekness, but the offer will remain open. Unless we find someone else."

They lean forward; a face pocketed by time and trial. "Captain, if I may be forward. I know what you are. Are you, really, not going to see this through?"
"I believe the survivors would be most helpful in your crusade. A heart of penance makes for a strong shield."

The Luddic commander is distant. There eyes are elsewhere, another time, far beyond the glow of their consoles.

"And it's done. Thank you, $playerName. Retribution has been delivered. You've done a great thing, here. And not just for the Church. For all mankind."

Just then, something rings in your ears. A distant, haunting gasp. It is not music, note even a note. Not even anything. Then, it is gone.

When you come to, you realize the Luddic commander is staring at you. "Captain?"

They return to their console, typing something unseen. "Hm. No major power detected. The demon that drove it is dead." They glance up, one eyebrow quirked. "We came here to kill the demon; that we have accomplished. I am...unsure, what we should do with its shell."

The destroyed ship lists through the void. The glowing squares of tracking sensor surround fires on every deck, errant amps pouring through the vessel's blasted components.

Whatever it is, or was, it is now dead.

As the buzz of the battle dies down in your bridge, you hear a faint mumbling behind you. You turn to find the Luddic envoy that'd come with you, their hands clasped in prayer.

"The Machine is dead," they state. "Hallelujah."
"You've done a great thing, Captain. That...thing." Their eyes shift, growing distant, pouring over the readouts of the dead hulk. "It was old. Quite old. Who knew what foul secrets it had to share."

Your head salvor speaks up. "Captain," he says. "Looks like whatever was piloting it is offline, but I think we just might be able to do something with that hulk." There's a quiet, but slightly maniacal tone to his voice. "Be somethin' to see."

The envoy narrows $hisOrHer eyes. "No. We came here to destroy the demon." He tone turns icy. "Completely," $heOrShe enunciates. "I will not stand for one atom of this abomination to remain. And neither will the Church."

text:
It is a thorough disassembly. The main guns of your largest ship roar upon the battered hulk for minutes on end. The dead ship begins to glow red, then blinding hot white. Its own body turns into a roaring inferno, fires spreading throughout as the superstructure begins to sag under the explosive torrent.

When a cease fire is ordered, the strange ship is little more than a vague, molten glob.

The Luddic Envoy balls $hisOrHer fists. "The Church has given you orders. Direct orders. You will destroy the demon's vessel."

Their stare is venom. They glare at you as if you were an Alpha core standing in front of them, then turn and storm out of the bridge.

A few minutes after they're gone, your tac officer turns to you, proverbial hat in hand.

"Uh, $SirOrMadame? Security one deck down just called. They said the envoy pushed her
way into an escape pod and, uh. Launched it."

They turn back to their console. "Tracking it now. We could intercept."
options:
0:exponentShootPod:Order the escape pod to be shot down
1:exponentLetPodGo:Let the envoy escape

text:
You order is nonverbal. A simple gesture, and your ship's weapons hum to half-waking.

When you walk over to the command console, you see the tracked escape pod on screen,
gently spinning through the void of space. A moment later, a potshot screams across its hull. The second shot grazes; the escpae pod is sent tumbling like a coin, debris and fuel spinning from its body in glittering arcs.

The third and final shot hits dead on, and the pod explodes in a puff of fire and broken metal.

You both stare at the expanding could of stellar flotsam.

"That's that," your tac officer huffs.

You give a wave; a silent order to let the envoy go.

"Are you sure, $SirOrMadame? They're not gonna be flattering if they get back to the
Church."
options:
0:exponentDestroyedPreRecover:"You have your orders, officer."
1:exponentDestroyedPreRecover:"It'll be fine."

text:
The head salvor chimes in.

"$SirorMadame, ready to start the recovery process. I'm not gonna lie, we might have to
improvise a bit with this one."

Your salvage teams get to work. It is a surprisingly smooth process, made simpler by the ship's relatively small size. Halfway through the process, the head salvor chimes in.

"Captain? We found the core housing. Whatever was piloting this thing is dead now, but, we're finding whole bunks and cabins in here. We'll have to rip out a lot of these cables worming every which-away, but I think this thing was meant to have a crew. Originally, anyway."

Your salvage team arrives at the various point of the vessel's hole, drones already pouring in a full torrent of data. There's chatter, small deliberations on who will enter first and where, then silence.

Complete silence. Your headset has gone dead, and the confused expressions of your nearby officers tell you that theirs have, too.

The lights go dead. Then your ship. The entire bridge is plunged into darkness, and the familiar hum of life support draws down like a great dying sigh. Your bridge crew remain professional, at their station but now tersely exchanging status reports and orders as they attempt to draw the ship back to life.

Your bridge turns red; the crimson glow of emergency power. A few consoles in the bridge eek to life, and your officers swarm around them. After a few tense moments, there is a great click inside the ship, and the red glow is banished to welcome, sterile light.

Your tactical officer turns around, confused as you are. "Sir. Something just tried to fry the power. On, uh. Every ship in our fleet."

They turn back, scratching the back of their head. The systems officer at their console
engages in a brief conversation with the, before tactical turns back with a grave look. "I don't
know what to tell you, $playerSirOrMadam. It looks like a virus, but...if it is, it's been spreading through our fleet for days. Weeks, maybe. Look like it's just been dormant until something gave it the go order."

The tactical officer looks around the bridge, then approaches you and whispers into your ear.

"One of our firewall layers had old Second AI War code on it. Whatever just happened, it was
close enough to CWF from back then to get tagged as malicious the second it popped out.
Only reason we're not a drifting wreck right now."

You nod, and bid the officer to return to his work. The bridge settles back into normalcy, and the clacking keystrokes of an incident report.

The full breadth of the shutdown slowly becomes clear. Every ship in your fleet lost power
simultaneously, all triggered by an emergency shutdown of their power plants. The report by your comms officer pinpoints a specific line of code that was inert unless remotely activated, but there was no way any of your crew could have engaged it without being caught; until very recently, your crew had no idea it was there.

A disturbing implication creeps into your mind. You go over which ships were actively communicating with the fleet when the power went out, and find only your own was transmitting, and the only one to make a fleet-wide transmission precisely 6.29 seconds before the power went dead.

Whatever did this, it came from your own ship.

Later, you receive a mysterious message in your inbox.

"APOLOGIES. MISTAKEN IDENTITY."

Its origin has been thoroughly scrubbed. You could never hope to trace it back.
Your salvage team arrives at the various point of the vessel's hole, drones already pouring in a full torrent of data. There's chatter, small deliberations on who will enter first, and where.

After the salvage team makes entry, there is a long period of silence. Radio feeds give back only gnarling static, and tactical starts looking worried.

Eventually, a voice pours through. The head of the salvage team, their voice garbled by interference. You can tell they're almost shouting through the snow, saying something about "passive EM".

Through the static, you hear something else. A note; a long series of them, almost-song
rapping at the back of your brain. With each second the tempo increases, smooth and gentle, louder and louder until it is a great hand knocking upon the bulkhead.

"Sir?"

You do a double-take. The music vanishes, dust on the wind, and you find yourself standing in front of your mildly-concerned chief engineer.

The chief engineer seems almost relieved as you look at them, then steps back and clears their throat. "As I was saying, I think we can get her flyin' again. I've heard..." They trail off, staring sideways into nothing before making a shrug. "Eh, nevermind."

Had you been asked a shift ago what you thought would be found at this location, the answers would vary; some long lost research facility, a trap set up by some forgotten black-ops unit, or more than likely nothing at all. The Onslaught Mk.I alone was an incredible find, and yet you've managed to reach further beyond- now stumbling upon a completely undocumented ancestor to the already venerable Legion.

You're dragged from your storming thoughts by your salvage chief clearing their throat. "Salvor teams are prepared and awaiting your command, $playerSirOrMadam."

You watch as small open-frame shuttles emerge from your fleet and lumber their way towards the Legion MK.I, loaded down with salvage equipment and crew, autonomous drones moving in to assist like flies towards a corpse. Entry into the vessel is no easy task; airlock doors and service hatches stubbornly refuse to yield to the usual assortment of prying tools and cutting torches, the ancient vessel holding its ground against your attempts to breach it. Having to resort to a concerningly powerful assortment of breaching charges placed strategically on armored doors, your crew are finally able to access the innards of the ship after quite the difficult fight.

Entering the gargantuan hull, your salvor teams, and by extension you via their suit-mounted cameras, are greeted by an eerily familiar sight. Electromechanical tendrils wormed throughout the ship, clinging to interfaces long ago built for human hands, now shifted by time into an alien form. Those who were present during the Onslaught Mk.I's recovery describe the innards of the Legion Mk.I and its automation systems as 'rounder', though notably almost identical to the crude automation you'd seen before. Hours pass by as the broken systems of the ship are gradually repaired and returned to operating order, though their commanding automation remains silent.

Weapon mounts have taken heavy fire, barrels of its Devastator cannons snapped off and mutilated. The ship's engines are coated by burn marks and patches of melted material, a signature indicator of having been pushed beyond their limit.

The most concerning of the battle damage is that which is unexplainable. Entire portions of armor plating and hull underneath are entirely missing, surgically removed in unpredictable chunks by some unknown force. The damage patterns are too clean to have been any laser, exposed uncorroded metal ruling out chemical weapons, perfect round edges excluding the possibility of explosives. It's as if pieces of the ship were deliberately stripped off and scrapped, but what could have done so this far into the Abyss? You don't have time to ponder the question, as your salvage chief looks to you and clears their throat, Tri-pad in hand.

"$PlayerSirOrMadam, we believe it's recoverable."

text:
Anxious murmuring slowly breaks loose the silence within your bridge. The metallic form before you so heavily damaged in so many ways, it makes even you wonder what could have possibly wrought such destruction upon a vessel as rugged in design as this primitive Dominator. Your sensors crew needs only to read your expression to rush to work, running high-power sweepscans and bringing together a detailed model for analysis.

Cannon barrels lay twisted and broken, one of the ship's disposable armor plates entirely missing, the other haphazardly splattered with impacts and pierced holes. Engines are scarred by burns and portions of melted components, a clear sign of being pushed well beyond their limits. Damage patterns even suggest the ship suffered a high-speed collision with a hard object- perhaps the hull of a ship.

Most concerning however, is the damage that your crew cannot identify. Significant chunks of armor plating and underlying hull have been stripped with unnerving precision- more smooth than any weapon impact you've seen. The metal below these missing portions is clean, uncorroded, nearly polished- far too clean for any explosive, laser, or even some form of acid based weapon. It appears almost as if pieces of the hull were cleanly stripped, yet the burn marks around conduits left exposed suggest the ship was active, and in fact at combat power, during this process. 

Crew look amongst themselves with nervous expressions, your salvage chief making hand movements said by old spacer superstition to be a seal of protection.

You watch as open-vacuum shuttles and salvage drones approach the drifting wreck, trundling through the suffocating darkness of the Abyss. Never before had lightless vacuum felt so thick, until you and your crew made that fateful voyage out chasing sensor ghosts, out finding what went bump in the night those 200 cycles ago. The irony is something not lost upon you, how you've repeated the same chase again. At least, this time, it isn't on the leash of some academia or corporation.

Your thoughts are interrupted by the dull click of shuttle anchors against bare metal, relayed from the salvagers' cameras to your main display. Entry into the vessel is no difficult task, numerous breaches throughout its hull making entry a trivial process. Salvors mumble among themselves, the interior of the ship revealing itself in structure both alien and not- familiar control consoles once manipulated by human hands, now overtaken by the same electromechanical infestation you've come to know.

Tendrils of steel and wire wrap themselves through corridors and around every station once manned by the vessel's brave crew, a form of automation so incredibly primitive it surprises you that the vessels hosting it can even navigate- let alone hold their own in combat. Those among the salvor crew present during the Onslaught Mk.I's exploration remark of the automation seeming 'sharper', and you can't help but agree- something about this vessel emanates a sort of malice, malevolence you can't describe even to yourself.

You overhear one salvor in particular swearing to their team they had heard the vessel itself growl at them, upon bumping into an exposed conduit. Others traverse the hull with hands closer than is usual to the few sidearms they carry, a general sense of anxious unease perforating the comm channels. Lucky charms are held close to chests in tightly clenched fists, seals of protection made with brief somatic movements among the more superstitious.

Recovery of the vessel is a laborious process. So many systems damaged or destroyed, connections between electromechanical components severed or shorted, the ship's reactor cold and dead for centuries. The stars have blessed you with great fortune though, it seems; enough remains of the vessel's data stores to reconstruct something abstractly describable as a blueprint. Still demanding much jury-rigging and patchwork from your crew, but just barely making the prospect of restarting the venerable monster more than a distant fantasy.

The moment the reactor is jumpstarted, low-power radio signals fill the hull with a warhorn song, tapping of solenoids against control panels louder than before observed nearly overburdening the sensitive acoustic monitors. Salvors barely have time to secure themselves to bulkheads, or whatever similar sturdy-looking protrusions they can find, before the Dominator Mk.I's engines roar back to life. text:
One of your bridge crew approaches you, nerviously clearing their throat to draw your attention. "$PlayerSirOrMadam, the report you ordered is ready. About the olds- Onslaught Mk.I's... movements."

Since being integrated into your fleet, the Onslaught Mk.I has displaying anomalous behavior. Turning and pointing in seemingly random directions when idle, leaving space for a ship not present during maneuvers, sending encrypted data over comms to nothing in particular. Your concerns were proven more than simple paranoia when the ship began moving on its own, wandering from formation before being noticed and swiftly ordered back into place, a command it followed as if it hadn't just been maneuvering by itself just mere seconds ago. Since that incident, the vessel has been under closer observation- and it seems your crew may have finally made a breakthrough.

You extend your hand, and quickly presented to you is a Tri-Pad. A full report, pages and pages worth of data and observations condensed down into only a few paragraphs for your own review. As your eyes move across the neatly arranged lines of text, the assistant begins to speak again.

"Sensors has been trying to decrypt the data transmissions- it's a step away from nonsense, but there is a pattern. We think it's telemetry data, the kind that automated ships broadcast to each other. And the movements- Nav has been going through logs, every time the ship moved on its own. We all thought it was random, some kind of malfunction, a gyroscope error or some flaw in its piloting, but- it's been pointing at two spots, every single time, without fail. A-at the bottom of the page, there, we noted down the coordinates-" She trails off, eyes wandering around the bridge, her body language straying from formal into the realm of anxiety.

Your attention is briefly drawn away from the report by anxious murmuring. Your head turns, and the crew now in your eyeline quickly straighten up and return to their work, the sound of boots shuffling against the metal flooring of the bridge spreading as others realize that you can, in fact, hear them. Your attention returns to the report, eyes running over the last line left unread- aforementioned triangulated locations. The reason for your crew's apprehension quickly becomes clear as you recognize the implications of these coordinates.

They're in the Abyss.

You get the impression they were intentionally kept in the dark about the vessel's rather illegal internals. Secrets become expontentially harder to keep the more mouths are running, and the Hegemony using an AI warfleet becoming public information would certainly shake up some of the leadership, even if said warfleet was deployed a hundred cycles ago.

Any Taskforce Safeguard vessels in your fleet are temporarily withdrawn from your fleet and escorted into a quiet and unassuming hangar bay at the edge of the dock, a small collection of trusted engineers prepared to accept them and versed in nearly forgotten Hegemony repair procedures.

It's unclear if such things still exist in a lonely fading manual on some dusty page, or if the techniques are passed on from one to the next. Regardless of the means the result is apparent in this moment.

text:
As your $shipOrFleet sends out its transponder code to dock with $market.name, you receive a request from the dock's portmaster to open a comm link.

Your ops chief gives you a knowing look - with the types of people who tend to end up in higher positions at the corporation, it's unlikely to be anything good. Your $shipOrFleet's transponder is already on, meaning dodging the request is rather pointless now.

Your comms are soon connected to the market's portmaster, who greets you stiffly. "Why, hello spacer," they proclaim in a rather nervous tone. Their vision flicks back and forth between the visual display and something off-screen. "I can't help but notice you have, well, something interesting in your fleet."
options:
0:nsp_TTMarketSafeguard2a:"Could you be more specific?"
20:nsp_TTMarketSafeguard2b:"Is there going to be a problem?"

text:
"Well," they pause, again briefly diverting away from the display. "The Hegemony ships. I believe they're Fourteenth Battlegroup, yes? But there's something, um, different. Isn't there?"

You get the impression it's more of a rhetorical question. Or one they hope you don't attempt to answer, at least.

"No, no, of course not. It's just that, well, um," they take a moment to check something on their TriPad. "There's someone who wants to speak with you about, well, your ships. The Fourteen Battlegroup ones."
They let out a sigh, realizing that skirting the issue isn't working. "Someone is very interested in the um, shall we say, 'altered' Fourteenth Battlegroup ship you have in your fleet."

A streak of surprise crosses the portmaster's face. "That's uh, very interesting. No, that won't be an issue. Not at all." they stammer out at your unexpected response.

"That's why we needed to speak with you, I believe"
"You're invited to Glamor Rotanev's office, on Eochu Bres. At your earliest convenience - we wouldn't want there to be any, well, problems. Not that there would be any problems, of course."

You know exactly who it is - after all, you've been in their presence before. But a little extra poking and prodding can never hurt. There's no telling what a frazzled employee may accidentally spill if they've been privy to private information, in any case.

"Director Rotanev is"

"She's interested in, well, um," the portmaster pauses before they trip over their words and fall into an HR meeting. "Things beyond the mundane, I believe is how she'd describe them. And you have something along those lines."

"Oh, so you've already been invited? I suppose, well, that's not surprising." They appear to visibly relax, just slightly. "Given you found... that, it's not completely out of the question that she already talked to you before."

"Oh, so you've already been invited? I suppose, well," a pause. "Wait, did you ask who she was? Did you forget?"

They sigh, eyes drifting away from the visual feed. "I find she's, um, rather hard to forget. In a way." A cough. "A good one, I assure you."

The portmaster sits up just a bit straighter in their seat after hearing you decline their offer. "Wait! Wait. Please don't misunderstand, this isn't a sales pitch. Just consider it - I'm certain the Director will make this mutually beneficial for you."

They quietly add on to the end of their statement, "I think."

As the portmaster is about to plead to you to consider their request, you cut them short and terminate the comm link.

They're certainly persistent, if anything.

"Fantastic. You've made a good decision for both of us."

They turn from the display and eagerly note something down. You imagine it's for their impending performance report.

"Yes!" they answer eagerly, before they catch themselves. "I mean, yes, our business is concluded. Please see the Director at your earliest convenience."

$HeOrShe quickly cuts the link before you can ask any more questions.

Director Zunya Glamor-Rotanev, her position evoking her full name to come to mind, seems mostly uninterested in conversation, a deadpan expression betraying a false attempt at a warm welcome.

"Ah you've arrived, $playerFirstName. I trust your fleet is holding together well? Though, you are here for business, being quite the practical individual. Do you have one of the ships with you?"

"And yet you didn't think to actually bring one? Incompetence or caution, matters little."

You feel colder than the vac. 

"Next time, bring me something worth my time before you try to beg for alms, $playerLastName."
"I see you brought one of them with you. Not tailed, I hope, by any unseemly visitors." She rolls her eyes, perhaps in show, "Of course, if you were, we would know, wouldn't we?"

"No?" The Director raises a brow, her face creased. "I begin to wonder why you've come to me to begin with, but knowing our previous arrangements you've surely still come with something interesting, yes?"

"Such interesting ships, $playerFirstName. I must ask, however, how you acquired them. The Hegemony might still have an interest in them, and as you'll know, the Sector doesn't fare well when the greater players butt heads."

The Director's eyes bore into you like tachyon lances, full of avarice and ambition, lined with suitable caution.

You describe your encounter with the automated vessels, giving more or less vague details with regards to the survivors on Sentinel and least of which the Planetkiller you went there to find to begin with. While Zunya notices your refusal to elaborate, she does not pursue it, being clearly more interested in the AI and the ships you found them in, especially the worn 14th Battlegroup livery that adorned them.

"And when you engaged this Taskforce Safeguard, did you find anything of importance besides the fleet itself following the battle?"

They give you an appraising look - you suspect they have at least an inkling of information regarding the planetkiller that was stowed away within the asteroid.

"Hm." They pause for a moment to give your statement some thought. "Interesting, and just as I had suspected."

"Very well then, onto our intended schedule for today."

The Director gives a dismissive wave of the hand. "No, not particularly - I was simply confirming one of my suspicions. If you've yet to do anything morally reprehensible with it, I'm certain other board members would be interested in a... mutually beneficial transaction."

"Such implements are far too mundane for us. Scorned worlds, AI warfleets prowling the fringes," she tiredly shakes her head. "The Sector is familiar with them - it's known. No, I'm after something truly extraordinary."
"Is that so? Disappointing."

"This is something that should not exist by all accounts, and yet, " she broadly gestures towards you, "here it is. I don't often care for remnants from the First AI War - most are far too common that one could wander into them on accident, I'm certain you know. But this?"

"It's a rather unique specimen. Not the AI alone, but rather the forbidden chalice containing it. An AI warfleet operating under the Hegemony's banner - they declared it the devil, then walked with it hand in hand. How interesting."

"I don't doubt that," the Director says rather matter-of-factly. "But if the information was to hypothetically be leaked without the extra details, well," she gives you a knowing look. "That would be rather interesting, don't you say?"

You consider what she's bluntly hinting at. Taskforce Safeguard was hurriedly assembled over a hundred cycles ago, in a desperate situation that may have warranted its deployment in the eyes of many at the time of its creation. The scars of the Second AI War are still plainly fresh on the sector, however -

"All that's required is for you to allow us access to one of the Taskforce Safeguard vessels. After we acquire the needed scans of the hull structure and," a pause, "other relevant systems, we should have the required data for our technicians to restore them for you. For a modest fee, of course."

"I believe we can come to an amicable agreement, $playerFirstName."

"Given our previous collaboration with a somewhat... similar type of hull, I trust we can come to an amicable agreement."

"Because," Rotanev turns a palm upwards, gesturing towards you. "There are riches waiting - you've not a need to lift a finger. Five hundred thousand credits, to be precise. Generous, is it not? You've nothing to lose, and we have both to gain."

text:
The capital-class construct appears to be a phase ship due to presenting features common to the type, though its design is otherwise exotic.

There also appear to be small, bright EM sources, "-Only partially overlapping the visual spectrum," your sensors officer reports. They periodically appear and dissipate in a volume encompassing the mysterious ship. Your bridge crew murmurs speculation between their stations: a new form of shielding? microsat thruster bursts? Your sensors officer shakes their head.

You order a high-resolution scan performed, and the raw data placed into secure storage.

Your attention strays as the impression of something not unlike distant music insinuates itself into your consciousness; as if a chorus was singing at some great distance, their voices brought to you by a chance gust of wind. When you attempt to focus on the music the impression slips away.

You become suddenly aware that your bridge crew is staring expectantly, waiting for your next command.

Your attention strays as the impression of something not unlike distant music insinuates itself into your consciousness; as if a chorus was singing at some great distance, their voices brought to you by a chance gust of wind. When you attempt to focus on the music the impression slips away.

You become suddenly aware that your bridge crew is staring expectantly, waiting for your next command.

A final terrific explosion blanks the external visual pickups. A few seconds later, backups are extruded through the hull.

Your sensors officer reports in a hushed voice that no escape pods were detected leaving the ship at any point.
The broken phase vessel, now quite dormant, is drifting through space.
Your salvage teams dock shuttles at various entry points along the vessel's massive hull.

After a few tense minutes, reports start to come in - the vessel is heavily damaged, and though of exotic design, it is theoretically recoverable.

Your operations chief reports that for all of the fancy hull features, it is clear that this ship requires crew to operate. But there are no traces of a crew, not even a single body caught in the battle damage, and the escape pods are all in their berths.

The operation proceeds with telemetry feeds, salvors' reports, and authorization orders flowing around you, through the bridge of your flagship. You catch yourself listening for that unheard music in a quiet moment, and shake your head just as a comms request from your technology officer appears, bringing you back from your reverie. You accept as a matter of course.

"$PlayerSirOrMadam, if I understand half of these systems, this ship is truly one of a kind," your technology officer speaks with genuine excitement.

"I've found a device that appears to generate and control - I'm not sure that either is the right word, really - these ... swarming motes, the EM anomalies. The device appears to have two stages, the first as I've described, and what appears to be a later addition which is, unfortunately, damaged beyond repair."

"Judging by the complexity of the components and the bizarre discharge pattern... this is the work of a team of specialists doing bleeding-edge work. It's amazing! A device like this, it's simply unheard of nowadays. Except," Tech looks abashed suddenly, "Rumors. You know, people talk."

Your technology officer clears their throat, then continues "I think I can get the main part of this device working again, though I can't claim to understand why it works. Not at all. The ship itself will be fit to fly, too, if we do the usual repairs. Should we proceed with recovery?"

The connection request hangs for some time then a wave of holo-noise flickers through the main display before generating a series of error codes. Your comms officer works their console in consternation. 

The soft sounds of the error notifications align just so, almost forming a melody you must have heard somewhere once. Or perhaps not. You return your attention to your command. No time for daydreaming.
